claims.text: Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 is initially in a high-temperature BCC state.
Annealing-induced short-range atomic ordering controls phase stability in Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7.
Short-range atomic ordering kinetically traps the high-temperature BCC phase when annealing is followed by rapid quenching.
The competition between diffusion-mediated local ordering or early precipitation during annealing and suppression of further transformation during rapid cooling determines BCC retention.
Annealing near 1100°C permits atomic rearrangement and development of short-range chemical order in the BCC matrix.
Short-range chemical ordering reduces local free energy.
The reduction in local free energy caused by ordering temporarily stabilizes BCC and retards transformation to equilibrium phases.
Extended annealing provides sufficient diffusion time to nucleate secondary phases.
Secondary phases initiated during extended annealing may grow during quenching.
Shorter annealing times followed by quenching will produce a more homogeneous retained BCC structure than longer annealing times.
Longer annealing intervals will produce incipient ordering and early-stage precipitation indicating transformation away from the BCC state.
A minimally or non-annealed sample preserves the nominal high-temperature BCC state without significant atomic ordering.
The proposed mechanism applies when annealing permits modest diffusion while remaining below the full equilibrium transformation range.
Quenching must be sufficiently rapid to freeze the annealed microstructure.
Large composition or processing changes that substantially alter diffusion kinetics fall outside the hypothesis's scope.
Comparable XRD, TEM, and APT results for long-annealed and minimally annealed samples would falsify the proposed ordering-mediated phase-stability hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The mechanism says secondary phases may grow during quenching, whereas the hypothesis and boundary condition characterize rapid quenching as suppressing further transformation and freezing the microstructure.
